newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore cabinet reshuffle meets mixed reaction.
newsitem.headline: Singapore cabinet reshuffle meets mixed reaction.

text.p: Political commentators in Singapore gave a mixed reaction on Sunday to a post-election cabinet reshuffle announced by Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong.
Goh's People's Action Party convincingly won a January 2 general election, picking up 81 of the 83 seats in the island republic's parliament. Goh announced the reshuffle late on Saturday.

The local Sunday Times newspaper saw the four-post reshuffle involving the Trade and Industry, Education, Health and Environment portfolios as preparation for the future, but other analysts were surprised that no new blood was introduced.

A Singapore-based European diplomat, who declined to be identified, told Reuters he was "quite surprised there are not more changes, especially as Goh has said he wanted to bring in the people who would lead the country into the next century".
Commentators agreed that the ministerial alterations would leave general policy unchanged.
The key moves, effective from January 25 when the government is sworn in, were seen at Trade and Industry and Education.
At Trade and Industry, Lee Yock Suan replaced Yeo Cheow Tong. Yeo was given back the Health brief he held in 1994 and also received the Environment portfolio.
Lee moved from Education to take over the role seen by analysts to have a heavy international profile as Singapore positions itself as a regional business hub.
In the January 2 poll, Lee led a team against the opposition Workers' Party in the fiercely contested Cheng San constituency.
Cheng San became the focus of the campaign after Goh accused an opposition candidate there of "Chinese chauvinism" which he said threatened the island's racial harmony.
Education was taken over by Teo Chee Hean, formerly at Environment. Teo, 42, has been said by Goh to be one of the younger ministers he sees at the core of government in the next century.

The appointment of new MP Peter Chen, the former chief executive of oil company Shell, as senior minister of state at education, was seen by observers to add weight to government aims to build links between business and education.

In the remaining change of cabinet responsibilities, George Yeo relinquished the Health portfolio to become Second Minister at the Trade and Industry ministry. He retains the job of Minister for Information and the Arts.

A government statement said more cabinet changes would be announced within two years, enabling the ministers for Communications and National Development to remain during the implementation of major programmes. No details were given.
